# Meanwhile...

The internet is strange. Some of that strangeness deserves to be enjoyed.

## Purpose

Meanwhile... is the publication's pressure valve. It finds funny, unexpected, wholesome, bizarre, or delightful moments online and gives readers a clean break from heavier coverage.

The section makes room for wonder and amusement without lowering the publication's standards.

## Reader expectation

Readers should find a brief story they want to send to someone. Get to the
moment quickly and give it enough context to make sense. Credit and link the
original creator.

The pleasure cannot depend on a false premise or someone's humiliation. A
playful headline must not hide serious harm.

## What belongs

- Unexpected acts of ingenuity or kindness.
- Bizarre internet subcultures and harmless disputes.
- Funny uses of technology.
- Small creative projects with outsized charm.
- Animals, objects, games, communities, or coincidences behaving in genuinely surprising ways.
- Internet artifacts that reveal something light and true about how people live online.
- Low-stakes mysteries whose pleasure lies in the search.

The item needs more than novelty. It should reward attention and survive a basic account of what really happened.

## What does not

- Hard news.
- Investigations.
- Tragedy repackaged as amusement.
- Public shaming of a private person.
- Harassment campaigns, dogpiles, or fandom conflict with real targets.
- Dangerous stunts presented without consequence.
- Hoaxes and staged moments passed off as spontaneous.
- Branded content disguised as an organic curiosity.
- A meme whose only context is that it is currently popular.

## Typical length

Most pieces run from 300 to 700 words. A single image, clip, or exchange may need less. A small internet mystery or reported subculture may run to 1,000 words when the reporting improves the fun.

Leave before the explanation drains the life from the story.

## Tone

Let the fun arrive quickly. Writers have more room for humor here than in other
sections, provided the facts remain sound and the subject keeps their dignity.

Forced meme language and exaggerated disbelief make the piece worse.

## Publishing philosophy

Verify the premise and find the earliest reliable source before writing. Credit
the creator and link to the original artifact when possible. Ask permission
when coverage would expose a private person or move their work far beyond its
intended audience.

Coverage can send a large audience toward a small account. Check the likely
effect before linking, protect personal information, and avoid turning a
private person into a target. Stop reporting once further explanation begins
to flatten the moment.

## Success metric

The section succeeds when it refreshes the reader and leaves the people inside the story no worse for having been covered.

Review a sample of stories for:

- accurate attribution and a working path to the original;
- corrections, takedown requests, or signs that coverage created unwanted attention;
- reader responses that identify the specific thing they enjoyed;
- a range of communities and forms rather than repeated dependence on the same large platforms;
- restraint during serious news cycles, when placement and timing can change how a light story feels.

Shares may show that a piece carried delight beyond the site. Editorial success still depends on truth, credit, and the treatment of its subjects.

## Internal examples

- A small online community recreates a lost digital object from memory. Credit
  the organizers and let their argument over tiny details carry the story.
- A programmer builds an impractical tool for one oddly specific household
  problem. Test it, then let the absurd precision supply the humor.
- An animal keeps appearing in a public webcam at the same point each day.
  Verify the footage and give readers the short version of the running joke.
- Two niche hobby groups use the same obscure equipment for unrelated
  purposes. Explain the coincidence without treating either group as an
  exhibit.

## Anti-examples

- A person's worst day reposted with a funny caption.
- A staged brand video described as an accidental viral moment.
- A hard-news event placed here because one detail sounds absurd.
- A joke built on a false translation or cropped exchange.
- A pile of reaction posts with no original source.
- A dangerous challenge covered in a way that helps readers repeat it.
- A sweet story stretched until every sentence asks the reader to feel something.
